Every litre of Jet A-1 at this airport passes through a fuel farm built to JIG standards. Its job: deliver clean, dry fuel, and prove it.
Step one, receipt. Fuel arrives by pipeline with a refinery certificate. It is filtered on the way in, and sampled against that certificate.
Step two, storage. Tank floors slope down to a sump. Water is heavier than fuel, so it sinks, settles, and is drained away.
Step three, release. Only after settling and a passed test does an authorised person release the tank for use.
Step four, filtration. A floating suction draws fuel from near the top. Filter water separators then strip out remaining water and dirt, while gauges monitor every filter.
Step five, delivery. Fuel flows through the underground hydrant network to the aircraft stand, and a dispenser filters it once more into the wing.
Every day, sumps are drained, samples must be clear and bright, and every result is recorded. Because water left in jet fuel can freeze at altitude, each step is a barrier.
